name: Hathi Grey
lede: Hathi Grey is a muted, slightly greenish grey filed by Robert Ridgway's 1912 color-standards system under a Hindi and Urdu word for elephant, though nothing in our sources says why Ridgway chose that word for this exact shade.

sections.title: An elephant's name, an undocumented reason
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 color-standards system is the earliest of our sources to record this swatch, plate LII, hue 35, tone b [1]. That makes it an older citation than the Maerz and Paul dictionary that supplies the earliest record for many other names in our library; no Maerz and Paul entry exists for Hathi Grey at all [1]. The word "hathi" means elephant in both Hindi and Urdu, and traces back further to Sanskrit *hastin*, "the one with a hand," a description of the trunk [2]. Whether Ridgway meant to evoke an elephant's hide specifically, or simply reached for a vivid, exotic-sounding word the way nineteenth and early-twentieth-century color systems often did, is not stated anywhere in the sources consulted here — the word's own meaning is documented; the namer's reasoning is not [1][2].

The real 1955 ISCC-NBS filing for the exact name Hathi Grey lands on block 155, "greenish gray" [3]. Ridgway's own cross-reference to the 1955 system, printed in his plate notes, points to the neighboring block 154 instead [1]. The two are close but not identical, a small, honest sign of how two legitimate readings of the same old plate can land one block apart.

sections.title: Its neighbors
sections.body: In the color graph, Hathi Grey sits 3.4 units from [[traffic-grey-a]], almost the same color, and 3.9 units from [[deep-gull-grey]], also almost indistinguishable [4]. [[greenish-grey]], 4.4 units off, is also almost the same, while [[dawn-grey]], also 4.4 off, is lighter [4]. [[olive-grey]], 4.9 off, and [[bluish-grey]], 5.2 off, both still read as close cousins rather than a different color [4]. That many near-identical neighbors in a tight cluster is typical of a muted, low-chroma grey: the eye has far less room to tell small differences apart than it does among saturated colors.

sections.title: Seen in
sections.body: Among design aesthetics, the closest full-palette matches are Tonalism, 1.6 units off on this exact swatch, and Romantic sublime, 2.2 off, also on Hathi Grey itself, with Cassette Futurism a step further at 3.1 units on its neighbor Olive-Grey [5]. Both of the two closest are period-appropriate: Tonalism and the Romantic sublime are both built on hazed, muted, atmospheric grays of roughly this same era [5]. On screen, Antonioni's *Red Desert*, a film built around industrial grey-on-grey, sits 4.6 units off, and Tati's *Playtime*, built around cool modernist architecture, sits 8.3 off [6]. In fashion, Pantone's 2021 Color of the Year pairing, Ultimate Gray and Illuminating, lands 6.5 units away, and Dior's own in-house grey, Dior grey, sits 8.9 off [7]. Three garments in our own archive land close by: a French dress 2.6 units off, a Lyon-made copy of a Zandaniji silk 3.4 off, and an Italian textile fragment from Perugia also 3.4 off [8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this grey in 699 of 23,778 paintings, about 2.9 percent as photographed; a stricter within-painting lens finds it in 430 [9]. That makes it more common than 80 percent of the named colors in the archive [9]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light tone, 47 percent of its 430 clearest matches, by lightness rank within each canvas so an aged varnish cannot fake the result [9].

Its most devoted painter, by how far he exceeds his own period's baseline, is Henri Matisse, carrying it in 9 of 50 works here, 6.9 times the predicted rate; Eugène Boudin is close behind, 9 of 48 works, 6.6 times predicted [9]. Impressionism as a movement is itself over-represented, 13 of 140 Impressionist works here, 3.4 times the expected rate, and the color shares canvases with Deep Neutral Grey and French Grey far more than chance alone would explain [9]. It peaks century-wide in the 1900s, 2.8 percent of 1,674 paintings from then, and the sharper single-decade peak is actually centuries earlier, the 1660s, 3.3 percent of 820 paintings, though with a smaller lift [9]. The earliest match in the archive is from 1399, with 592 dated paintings carrying it through to 1950; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first, and a 1399 match sits 513 years before the name's own earliest record, Ridgway's 1912 system — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof that anyone named or mixed this exact grey that early [9]. This is a computed color match on photographed, varnished canvases, not a pigment test.

questions.answer: Two legitimate readings of the same old plate can land one block apart

openers: Hathi Grey is named for the Hindi and Urdu word for elephant, but nobody recorded why.
Henri Matisse reached for this exact muted grey nearly seven times as often as his peers did.

issues: Depth wave pilot: no book concordance exists for this name, so depth comes entirely from measured data (the color graph, archive fieldnotes, aesthetics-graph twins) plus one hedged web source for the word's own etymology. States plainly that Ridgway's specific reason for the name is undocumented.
